title: Relational division for analytical questions
description: A practical guide to finding entities that satisfy every requirement in a reference set, using a small hypothetical dataset, counterexamples, and SQL patterns for relational division.
lead: Some analytical questions are not asking whether an entity matches any condition. They are asking whether it matches every requirement in a reference set. Relational division is the relational pattern behind questions like: which customers bought every required category, which stores carry every mandatory item, or which accounts completed every onboarding step?

sections.heading: The question relational division answers
paragraphs: Relational division answers a precise question: given a set of candidate entities and a set of required values, which entities are associated with all required values? The word all is the important part. A normal join is good at finding matches. Relational division is about proving there are no missing required matches.

In analytical work, this pattern appears more often than the name suggests. Examples include customers who purchased every product category in a campaign, warehouses that stocked every required SKU, employees who completed every required training module, vendors that passed every required certification, and devices that emitted every expected event type during a test window.

The input shape has three logical parts. First, a candidate entity set, such as customers. Second, a reference set of requirements, such as required categories. Third, an association relation that records which entity has which value, such as customer-category purchases. The output is the subset of candidate entities for which every requirement has a corresponding association row.

This article uses a small hypothetical retail dataset. The goal is not to tune a specific SQL engine. The goal is to make the relational semantics visible, including counterexamples that commonly produce wrong analytical results.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture
paragraphs: Assume a retailer defines a starter-kit promotion. A customer qualifies only if they bought at least one item from each required category: batteries, charger, and case. Buying extra categories is allowed. Buying the same qualifying category more than once should not compensate for a missing category.

The relations below are intentionally small. The customer table defines the candidate entities. The required_categories relation defines the divisor, or the set of requirements. The customer_category_purchases relation defines observed associations between customers and categories. In a durable model, candidate keys should protect the grains that matter: one customer row per customer, one required row per program and category, and purchase/event rows at their actual event grain. The article on candidate keys and alternate keys is useful background for that modeling prerequisite.
The SQL is illustrative and written in a PostgreSQL-style common table expression form. It is meant to show the semantics, not to claim execution results from a live database.
bullets: Customer 201 bought all three required categories and should qualify.
Customer 202 has three qualifying-looking purchase rows but is missing case, so should not qualify.
Customer 203 bought all three required categories plus headphones; extra categories should not disqualify the customer.
Customer 204 is missing charger and should not qualify.
Customer 205 bought all three required categories with a duplicate case row and should qualify.
Customer 206 has no purchases and should not qualify while the requirement set is non-empty.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
customers(customer_id) AS (
  VALUES (201), (202), (203), (204), (205), (206)
),
required_categories(category) AS (
  VALUES ('batteries'), ('charger'), ('case')
),
customer_category_purchases(customer_id, category) AS (
  VALUES
    (201, 'batteries'),
    (201, 'charger'),
    (201, 'case'),

    (202, 'batteries'),
    (202, 'batteries'),
    (202, 'charger'),

    (203, 'batteries'),
    (203, 'charger'),
    (203, 'case'),
    (203, 'headphones'),

    (204, 'batteries'),
    (204, 'case'),

    (205, 'case'),
    (205, 'charger'),
    (205, 'batteries'),
    (205, 'case')
)
SELECT *
FROM customers;

sections.heading: Why any-match logic is not enough
paragraphs: The most common mistake is to convert an all-requirements question into an any-match query. For example, a join from purchases to required categories finds customers who bought at least one required category. That is useful for a funnel entry question, but it is not relational division.

In the hypothetical data, customers 201, 202, 203, 204, and 205 all bought at least one required category. Only 201, 203, and 205 bought every required category. If a dashboard labels the any-match result as qualified customers, it will overcount by including 202 and 204.

A second common mistake is counting rows instead of counting distinct requirements satisfied. Customer 202 has three purchase rows that match the required set: batteries, batteries, and charger. A naive count can make 202 look complete because three rows match three required categories. But the missing category is case. Multiplicity is not coverage.

This is why the grain of the association relation matters. Purchases are events. Requirements are categories. A customer can have many events for the same category, but the qualification rule is about distinct required categories covered by each customer.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
customers(customer_id) AS (
  VALUES (201), (202), (203), (204), (205), (206)
),
required_categories(category) AS (
  VALUES ('batteries'), ('charger'), ('case')
),
customer_category_purchases(customer_id, category) AS (
  VALUES
    (201, 'batteries'), (201, 'charger'), (201, 'case'),
    (202, 'batteries'), (202, 'batteries'), (202, 'charger'),
    (203, 'batteries'), (203, 'charger'), (203, 'case'), (203, 'headphones'),
    (204, 'batteries'), (204, 'case'),
    (205, 'case'), (205, 'charger'), (205, 'batteries'), (205, 'case')
)
SELECT p.customer_id
FROM customer_category_purchases p
JOIN required_categories r
  ON r.category = p.category
GROUP BY p.customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM required_categories)
ORDER BY p.customer_id;

-- This naive row-count pattern would include customer 202,
-- even though customer 202 is missing the required category 'case'.

sections.heading: The NOT EXISTS pattern
paragraphs: A direct way to express relational division in SQL is a double NOT EXISTS predicate. Read it in plain language: return customers for whom there does not exist a required category for which there does not exist a matching purchase. In shorter terms: there is no missing requirement.

This pattern keeps the universal condition visible. The inner NOT EXISTS asks whether a specific required category is missing for a specific customer. The outer NOT EXISTS keeps only customers for whom that missing-requirement search finds nothing.

For the hypothetical fixture, the expected result is customers 201, 203, and 205. Customer 201 has batteries, charger, and case. Customer 203 has batteries, charger, and case; headphones is irrelevant because it is not in the requirement set. Customer 205 has all three required categories; the duplicate case row does not matter. Customers 202, 204, and 206 each have at least one missing requirement.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
customers(customer_id) AS (
  VALUES (201), (202), (203), (204), (205), (206)
),
required_categories(category) AS (
  VALUES ('batteries'), ('charger'), ('case')
),
customer_category_purchases(customer_id, category) AS (
  VALUES
    (201, 'batteries'), (201, 'charger'), (201, 'case'),
    (202, 'batteries'), (202, 'batteries'), (202, 'charger'),
    (203, 'batteries'), (203, 'charger'), (203, 'case'), (203, 'headphones'),
    (204, 'batteries'), (204, 'case'),
    (205, 'case'), (205, 'charger'), (205, 'batteries'), (205, 'case')
)
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM required_categories r
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM customer_category_purchases p
    WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND p.category = r.category
  )
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

-- Expected customer_id values: 201, 203, 205

sections.heading: The COUNT DISTINCT pattern
paragraphs: Another common formulation groups by entity and compares the number of distinct required values satisfied with the number of required values. For many analytical readers, this is easier to inspect than the double negative. It also makes the distinction between row count and requirement coverage explicit.

The key is to count distinct required categories after joining purchases to the reference set. Counting purchase rows is wrong when duplicates exist. Counting distinct purchased categories without joining to the reference set can also be wrong if extra categories are present. The count should represent required categories covered, not all categories observed.

The basic version below works for a non-empty requirement set. It returns the same expected customers for this fixture: 201, 203, and 205. If the requirement set can be empty, decide the business rule explicitly. In formal relational division, every candidate entity satisfies an empty set of requirements because there is nothing missing. Some business processes instead treat an empty requirement set as a configuration error. Do not let that case be accidental.
bullets: Use COUNT(DISTINCT r.category), not COUNT(*), when event duplicates are possible.
Join observed values to the requirement set before counting, so extra categories do not inflate coverage.
Handle the empty-reference-set case deliberately.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
customers(customer_id) AS (
  VALUES (201), (202), (203), (204), (205), (206)
),
required_categories(category) AS (
  VALUES ('batteries'), ('charger'), ('case')
),
customer_category_purchases(customer_id, category) AS (
  VALUES
    (201, 'batteries'), (201, 'charger'), (201, 'case'),
    (202, 'batteries'), (202, 'batteries'), (202, 'charger'),
    (203, 'batteries'), (203, 'charger'), (203, 'case'), (203, 'headphones'),
    (204, 'batteries'), (204, 'case'),
    (205, 'case'), (205, 'charger'), (205, 'batteries'), (205, 'case')
),
required_count AS (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_required
  FROM required_categories
)
SELECT p.customer_id
FROM customer_category_purchases p
JOIN required_categories r
  ON r.category = p.category
GROUP BY p.customer_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT r.category) = (SELECT n_required FROM required_count)
ORDER BY p.customer_id;

-- Expected customer_id values for this non-empty requirement set: 201, 203, 205

sections.heading: Diagnose missing requirements before publishing the metric
paragraphs: A relational division query returns the entities that pass. Before publishing the metric, it is often more useful to inspect the entities that fail and the specific requirements they are missing. The diagnostic query is the complement: create every candidate-requirement pair, then remove the pairs that have a matching association row.

For the fixture, the missing pairs are straightforward. Customer 202 is missing case. Customer 204 is missing charger. Customer 206 is missing batteries, charger, and case. Customers 201, 203, and 205 have no missing required categories.

This diagnostic is also a modeling check. If the missing list is surprisingly large, the issue might be a real business outcome, but it might also be a grain mismatch, a category mapping problem, a stale reference set, or an association table that is filtered to the wrong time window. Relational division makes these assumptions visible because the query must name the candidate set, the requirement set, and the association relation.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
customers(customer_id) AS (
  VALUES (201), (202), (203), (204), (205), (206)
),
required_categories(category) AS (
  VALUES ('batteries'), ('charger'), ('case')
),
customer_category_purchases(customer_id, category) AS (
  VALUES
    (201, 'batteries'), (201, 'charger'), (201, 'case'),
    (202, 'batteries'), (202, 'batteries'), (202, 'charger'),
    (203, 'batteries'), (203, 'charger'), (203, 'case'), (203, 'headphones'),
    (204, 'batteries'), (204, 'case'),
    (205, 'case'), (205, 'charger'), (205, 'batteries'), (205, 'case')
)
SELECT c.customer_id, r.category AS missing_category
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN required_categories r
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM customer_category_purchases p
  WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND p.category = r.category
)
ORDER BY c.customer_id, r.category;

-- Expected missing pairs:
-- 202, case
-- 204, charger
-- 206, batteries
-- 206, case
-- 206, charger

sections.heading: Modeling assumptions that change the answer
paragraphs: Relational division is simple only after the relations are well defined. Most wrong answers come from unclear inputs, not from the SQL pattern itself.

The first assumption is the candidate set. If the query starts from the purchase table, customers with no purchases disappear before the all-requirements logic runs. That may be acceptable for some questions, but it is not equivalent to starting from all eligible customers. In the example, customer 206 must be present in the candidate set to be correctly evaluated as not qualified.

The second assumption is the requirement set. Requirements should be unique at the intended grain. If the same required category appears twice for the same program, count-based formulations can become ambiguous. A primary key or unique constraint on the requirement grain is the modeling protection. PostgreSQL documentation describes primary key, unique, and foreign key constraints as mechanisms for enforcing table-level rules; the same design idea applies regardless of the specific database product.

The third assumption is the association grain. If the association table records purchase events, duplicates are expected and should not imply additional coverage. If the association table is already a deduplicated customer-category bridge, the division query becomes simpler, but the bridge must be built with a clear grain.

The fourth assumption is the comparison value. Category names, codes, or identifiers must be comparable between the requirement relation and the association relation. If one table uses product category names and another uses SKU-level events, an intermediate mapping is needed before relational division is meaningful. That mapping problem is separate from the division operation itself.

Finally, define the treatment of nulls and unknowns before relying on the result. A null category is not evidence that a customer satisfied a specific required category. If unknown, invalid, and not-applicable values have business meaning, they should be modeled deliberately rather than allowed to leak into the division predicate.

sections.heading: When to use this pattern
paragraphs: Use relational division when the English version of the requirement says every, all, each, complete, covered, or no missing. It is especially useful for eligibility, compliance, coverage, and completion metrics.

Do not use it when the question is about any activity, the first matching event, the most recent status, or a threshold that does not require coverage of a named reference set. A customer who bought at least three items is not the same as a customer who bought one item from each of three required categories. A store with ten stocked SKUs is not necessarily a store with every mandatory SKU.

A good practical test is to ask whether you can produce a missing-requirements report. If the answer is yes, the problem likely has a relational division shape. If there is no meaningful list of missing requirements, a simpler join, aggregation, or ranking query may be the better model.
bullets: Name the candidate entity set.
Name the requirement set.
Name the association relation that can prove coverage.
Return entities with no missing required associations.
Keep a diagnostic query that shows the missing associations.

takeaways: Relational division finds entities associated with every value in a reference set; it is the right pattern for all-requirements questions.
Counting rows is a common counterexample failure because duplicate events can hide missing requirements. Count distinct required values or use a no-missing-requirements predicate.
A missing-requirements diagnostic is the best companion to the final qualified-entities query because it exposes grain, reference-set, and mapping problems before a metric is published.

title: Floating-point error in financial analytics
description: A practitioner guide to demonstrating representation error when decimal financial values are stored and aggregated as binary floating-point numbers.
lead: Repeated decimal arithmetic can make a financial dataset look inconsistent even when every row was loaded successfully. The core problem is not that computers are careless with money; it is that many decimal fractions do not have an exact finite representation in binary floating-point. This guide shows how to demonstrate that error with a small hypothetical retail example, separate representation error from rounding policy, and write diagnostics that make the risk visible before it reaches a dashboard or reconciliation process.

sections.heading: The specific problem: repeated decimals stored approximately
paragraphs: Financial analytics often starts with ordinary-looking decimal values: 0.10 dollars of loyalty credit, 1.25 dollars of delivery fee, 19.99 dollars of merchandise revenue. Some of those values are exactly representable in binary floating-point and some are not. The difference matters when a pipeline stores the values in an approximate numeric type and then repeats arithmetic across many rows.

A binary floating-point value represents numbers as a sign, a significand, and a power of two. That means finite binary fractions have denominators that are powers of two. The decimal value 0.25 is 1 divided by 4, so it can be represented exactly because 4 is 2 squared. The decimal value 0.125 is 1 divided by 8, so it can also be represented exactly. The decimal value 0.10 is 1 divided by 10. Since 10 includes a factor of 5, 1/10 cannot be written as a finite fraction whose denominator is only a power of two. A binary floating-point system must store a nearby value instead.

That nearby value is usually close enough for measurement, simulation, or ranking use cases. It is not the same as the decimal value, though. When a financial analytic repeatedly adds that approximate value, the aggregate is built from approximations. The resulting error may be tiny, but it is real, explainable, and capable of surprising downstream consumers when equality checks, joins, threshold filters, or reconciliation reports assume exact decimal arithmetic.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail counterexample
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail promotion table with one row per earned loyalty credit. Each qualifying event creates a 10-cent credit. The table has 10,000 events for the day. The business question is simple: how many dollars of credit were earned?

Using exact decimal arithmetic, the calculation is straightforward. Each event is 0.10 dollars. There are 10,000 events. The exact total is 10,000 multiplied by 0.10, which equals 1,000.00 dollars. If the same fact is stored as integer cents, each row stores 10 cents, and the exact total is 10,000 multiplied by 10 cents, which equals 100,000 cents, or 1,000.00 dollars.

Now compare that with the value commonly used by a binary double-precision representation for the decimal literal 0.1. The stored value is not exactly 0.1. Written as a decimal expansion, it is approximately 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625. That means the stored value is larger than the intended decimal value by approximately 0.0000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625 dollars per row.

If 10,000 rows all carry that same represented value, the representation error in the inputs alone is approximately 0.000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625 dollars. That is about 5.55e-14 dollars. This is far below a cent, so it is not a claim that the example creates a material financial misstatement. The point is narrower and more useful for data engineers: the aggregate is not mathematically identical to the exact decimal aggregate. Repeated decimal arithmetic has created a measurable difference before any business rounding rule is even discussed.

This counterexample also explains why the defect can hide during casual inspection. If a report formats the result to two decimal places, both the exact total and the approximate total display as 1000.00. If another job compares the unrounded floating-point result to an exact decimal target, the same data can fail an equality check. The visual presentation looks harmless while the stored value and the comparison semantics remain different.
bullets: Hypothetical rows: 10,000 loyalty-credit events.
Intended amount per row: 0.10 dollars, or exactly 10 cents.
Exact aggregate: 10,000 × 0.10 = 1,000.00 dollars.
Representative binary double input value for 0.1: approximately 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625.
Input representation error across 10,000 rows: approximately 0.000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625 dollars.

sections.heading: Calculation rules for a clean demonstration
paragraphs: A useful demonstration should isolate representation error from other concerns. Do not mix it with sales tax rules, invoice rounding rules, foreign exchange rules, or accounting policy. Those are separate topics. The goal here is to prove that repeated decimal arithmetic over approximate values can diverge from exact decimal arithmetic even when the source rows are conceptually simple.

Use four calculation rules. First, choose a decimal fraction that is not exactly representable in binary, such as 0.10. Second, define the exact value in a representation that is unambiguous, such as integer cents or a rational expression like 1/10. Third, state the approximate stored value separately from the business value. Fourth, compare aggregates before applying display rounding.

These rules prevent a common but misleading explanation: “the database rounded the money wrong.” In the hypothetical example, the database has not necessarily applied a two-decimal-place rounding policy at all. The issue is earlier. The value being aggregated is an approximate binary representation of a decimal amount. Rounding to cents at the end may hide the difference for a dashboard, but it does not make the intermediate arithmetic exact.

The clean demonstration also needs a counterexample in the other direction. Not every decimal-looking value is unsafe for binary representation. A 25-cent credit, 0.25 dollars, equals 1/4 and is exactly representable in binary. If the same hypothetical retailer issued 10,000 credits of 0.25 dollars, the exact total would be 2,500.00 dollars, and the per-row representation error for 0.25 would be zero. This contrast helps teams avoid the vague rule that “decimals are bad.” The precise rule is that many base-10 fractions, including common financial amounts such as 0.10, cannot be represented exactly as finite base-2 fractions.
bullets: Keep the demonstration to numeric representation and aggregation.
Use exact cents or rational arithmetic as the comparison standard.
Inspect values before presentation rounding, not only after formatting to two decimal places.
Include an exactly representable value, such as 0.25, to show that the issue is representation-specific rather than mystical.

sections.heading: A diagnostic pattern for pipelines
paragraphs: A practical diagnostic compares two aggregates that should describe the same business fact: one aggregate from the approximate amount and one aggregate from an exact representation. The exact side can be integer minor units, such as cents, or a fixed-point decimal column chosen for the required range and scale. The diagnostic is not meant to decide the final accounting treatment. It is meant to expose whether approximate arithmetic has entered a financial metric path.

The following SQL is illustrative for PostgreSQL 18 semantics, not supplied as execution evidence. PostgreSQL documentation distinguishes exact numeric types from inexact floating-point types, and its aggregate documentation describes aggregate behavior by input type. The pattern is to aggregate both representations and report the difference. In a real model, the fixture would be replaced with a staging table, event table, or ledger-like fact table.

The important part is the comparison shape: count the rows, sum the approximate dollars, sum the exact cents, convert the exact cents to dollars for readability, and compute the difference. If this diagnostic is used in a data quality job, do not use exact equality on floating-point values as the pass/fail condition. Either prohibit approximate numeric types in financial metric inputs or compare within an explicitly documented tolerance for non-financial measurement data. For currency-like facts, the more robust modeling move is usually to keep the source of record in integer minor units or an exact decimal type and reserve floating point for derived analytical calculations where approximation is acceptable.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL 18 diagnostic pattern; not execution evidence.
-- The dataset is hypothetical.
with hypothetical_loyalty_credits as (
  select *
  from (values
    (1, 10, 0.10::double precision),
    (2, 10, 0.10::double precision),
    (3, 10, 0.10::double precision),
    (4, 10, 0.10::double precision)
  ) as v(event_id, credit_cents, credit_dollars_float)
)
select
  count(*) as event_count,
  sum(credit_dollars_float) as float_dollar_sum,
  sum(credit_cents)::numeric / 100 as exact_dollar_sum_from_cents,
  sum(credit_dollars_float) - ((sum(credit_cents)::numeric / 100)::double precision) as float_minus_exact
from hypothetical_loyalty_credits;

sections.heading: Where the error becomes operational
paragraphs: For the 10,000-row loyalty-credit example, the representation error is far below a cent. That does not mean it is irrelevant to data engineering. The operational failures usually come from assumptions around exactness, not from the dollar size of the raw representation error.

One failure mode is an equality check between systems. Suppose a reconciliation job compares an exact decimal total from a payment processor with a floating-point total from an analytics table. If the job expects exact equality, it can flag a false mismatch. Another failure mode is a threshold rule. A segment definition such as “customers with credit balance equal to 100.00” is brittle if one side of the comparison is approximate. A third failure mode is a join key or grouping key derived from a floating-point calculation. Values that print the same at two decimal places may not be identical at the stored numeric level.

The diagnostic response should match the risk. For source-of-record financial facts, prevent the risk by modeling amounts as integer minor units or exact numeric values. For exploratory analytics that intentionally use floating-point measures, make comparisons tolerant and avoid using computed floats as identifiers. For published financial metrics, document the representation used for stored values, the aggregation type, and the stage at which any display rounding occurs.

This article intentionally stops before two adjacent design questions. It does not choose precision and scale for fixed-point decimal columns, and it does not decide whether rounding belongs at ingestion, transformation, or presentation. Those decisions require their own examples because they involve capacity, intermediate calculations, and reconciliation policy. The narrower lesson here is that representation error exists before those policies are applied.
bullets: False reconciliation mismatches can occur when exact and approximate aggregates are compared with equality.
Threshold filters can behave unexpectedly when a value that displays as 100.00 is stored as a nearby approximation.
Computed floating-point values are poor join keys for financial facts.
Formatting to two decimal places is presentation, not proof that the stored aggregate is exact.

sections.heading: A decision rule for financial analytics models
paragraphs: Use approximate floating-point types when the business fact is inherently approximate or when small representation differences are acceptable for the analytic purpose. Examples include sensor measurements, statistical features, and ratios where tolerance is part of the interpretation. Be more cautious when the business fact is a currency amount, fee, credit, balance, invoice line, or other value that users expect to reconcile exactly.

A simple decision rule is: if the value will be reconciled, invoiced, posted, audited, or compared for equality as money, do not make binary floating-point the authoritative representation. Store the exact fact first. Aggregate from that exact fact. Convert for presentation only after the calculation rules are clear. If a floating-point derivative is useful for modeling or visualization, make it a derivative rather than the source of record.

The demonstration is small by design. Ten thousand rows of 10-cent credits are enough to prove the representation issue without relying on a benchmark, a production story, or an exotic edge case. Once a team understands that proof, the modeling conversation becomes clearer: the question is not whether the observed difference is visually large in one report, but whether the data model preserves the numeric semantics that downstream financial analytics assume.

takeaways: Many common decimal financial values, including 0.10, cannot be represented exactly as finite binary floating-point numbers.
Repeated aggregation can preserve and expose tiny representation errors even when the final formatted report still displays the expected two-decimal total.
A clean diagnostic compares approximate aggregates with exact cents or exact decimal aggregates before display rounding.
For financial facts that must reconcile or support equality comparisons, store the authoritative value in integer minor units or an exact numeric representation rather than binary floating point.

title: Fixed-point decimal precision and scale
description: A practical guide to choosing decimal precision and scale for stored facts and intermediate calculations, with capacity rules and a worked hypothetical retail example.
lead: Fixed-point decimal types are usually chosen to avoid binary floating-point surprises, but exact representation is only half of the problem. Data engineers also have to choose enough precision and scale for values that are stored, multiplied, subtracted, and aggregated later. The common mistake is sizing a column for a single row while forgetting the larger intermediate values created by calculations.

sections.heading: What precision and scale actually control
paragraphs: For a fixed-point decimal declared as DECIMAL(p, s), precision p is the total number of significant decimal digits and scale s is the number of digits to the right of the decimal point. The number of digits available to the left of the decimal point is p minus s. DECIMAL(12, 2), for example, can represent two fractional digits and up to ten integer digits, so values such as 9999999999.99 are within the declared shape while 10000000000.00 is not.

That simple p minus s rule is the starting point for capacity planning. Scale answers the question: how small is the unit I need to preserve? Precision answers a wider question: how many total digits must fit after I reserve those fractional digits? If the business process produces large whole-number totals and also needs fine fractional detail, both sides compete for the same precision budget.

This article is about sizing, not accounting policy. It does not decide whether a discount, fee, tax, or allocation should be rounded at a particular business stage. The narrower engineering question is: once the required unit and business maximum are known, what decimal capacity should the stored columns and intermediate expressions have?
bullets: Use scale for the required fractional unit: cents require scale 2; basis-point-like rates often require scale 4; derived ratios may need more.
Use integer digits for the largest expected magnitude before the decimal point.
Use precision as the sum of those two capacities: required precision equals integer digits plus scale.
Do not size only for today’s observed maximum. Size for the documented domain, contractual limit, or an explicit operational cap.

sections.heading: Capacity rules for common expressions
paragraphs: A useful planning model is to track two numbers for every value: i for integer digits and s for fractional digits. A DECIMAL(p, s) has i = p - s. You can then reason about expression capacity before choosing the final column type.

For addition and subtraction, align to the larger scale. If two same-sign values can be added, allow one extra integer digit for carry. A conservative rule for a + b is: result scale equals max(sa, sb), and result integer digits equal max(ia, ib) + 1. If business constraints prove the result cannot grow, you may use a smaller bound, but the constraint should be real and documented. For example, gross minus a discount bounded between zero and gross does not need a carry digit for the business result, even if a generic SQL expression planner may allocate one internally.

For multiplication, fractional scale is the sum of operand scales before any later rounding or casting. Integer capacity can be derived from operand bounds. A conservative type-only rule is: result scale equals sa + sb, and result integer digits are at most ia + ib. This upper bound is sometimes wider than the real business domain, especially when multiplying by a rate constrained between 0 and 1.

For aggregation, the important mistake is forgetting row count. If the maximum positive row value has i integer digits and you may sum up to n positive rows, the sum can require i + ceil(log10(n)) integer digits. This is a safe digit-count rule for positive values of the same sign. It is sometimes conservative at powers of ten or when the row maximum is far below the largest value with i digits, but it is a good design rule because it connects capacity to a stated maximum row count.

Averages are not exempt. The final average may be smaller than the sum, but the sum used to compute it still needs aggregate capacity. If an engine computes AVG through an internal sum and count, the intermediate sum shape matters even when the output is later cast to a smaller display type.
bullets: Addition or subtraction: keep the larger scale; add an integer carry digit unless constraints rule it out.
Multiplication: add scales; bound the integer side from operand maxima, not from wishful typical values.
Sum: add enough integer digits for the maximum number of rows in the group.
Average: size the intermediate sum and choose a deliberate output scale for the average.

sections.heading: Worked example: hypothetical retail order lines
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order-line fact table. The example is intentionally small enough to audit by hand, but the maxima are large enough to show why intermediate capacity matters.

Assume quantity is a whole number from 0 through 9,999. That needs four integer digits and scale zero, so DECIMAL(4, 0) is sufficient for the stored quantity. Assume unit_price is from 0.00 through 999999.99. That needs six integer digits and two fractional digits, so DECIMAL(8, 2) is sufficient for the stored price.

The gross line amount is quantity multiplied by unit_price. The largest possible value is 9,999 multiplied by 999,999.99, which equals 9,998,999,900.01. That result has ten integer digits and two fractional digits. The multiplication rule also gives scale 0 + 2 = 2 and at most 4 + 6 = 10 integer digits. Therefore DECIMAL(12, 2) is the minimum shape for this gross amount under the stated assumptions.

Now add a discount_rate stored as DECIMAL(5, 4), but with a business constraint that it must be between 0.0000 and 1.0000. The type alone could hold values up to 9.9999, but the business constraint is narrower. The exact discount amount before any final presentation rounding is gross_amount multiplied by discount_rate. The fractional scale is 2 + 4 = 6. Because the rate is bounded at 1.0000, the discount cannot exceed the gross amount. It needs ten integer digits and six fractional digits, or DECIMAL(16, 6).

The net amount is gross_amount minus discount_amount. With the stated constraint that discount is between zero and gross, net is also between zero and gross. To preserve the six fractional digits introduced by the rate multiplication, a stored exact net such as line_net_exact should be DECIMAL(16, 6). If a downstream mart also stores a cents-level net amount, that smaller value is a separate presentation or settlement decision, not a reason to under-size the calculation field.

Finally, consider a daily revenue aggregate that may include up to 2,000,000 positive order lines. The largest line_net_exact is less than or equal to 9,998,999,900.010000. The line value needs ten integer digits. The maximum row count adds ceil(log10(2,000,000)) = 7 more integer digits. A daily sum therefore needs 17 integer digits and six fractional digits: DECIMAL(23, 6). The arithmetic check is 9,998,999,900.01 multiplied by 2,000,000, which equals 19,997,999,800,020,000.00, a 17-digit integer part.

If the monthly aggregate can include 62,000,000 lines, the row-count term is ceil(log10(62,000,000)) = 8. The monthly sum needs 18 integer digits and six fractional digits, or DECIMAL(24, 6). The maximum gross arithmetic is 9,998,999,900.01 multiplied by 62,000,000, which equals 619,937,993,800,620,000.00, an 18-digit integer part.
bullets: quantity: DECIMAL(4, 0), because the maximum is 9,999.
unit_price: DECIMAL(8, 2), because the maximum is 999999.99.
line_discount_exact: DECIMAL(16, 6), because multiplying by a scale-4 rate creates six fractional digits.
daily_revenue_exact for up to 2,000,000 lines: DECIMAL(23, 6).
monthly_revenue_exact for up to 62,000,000 lines: DECIMAL(24, 6).

codeExamples.code:
Hypothetical capacity worksheet

Stored values:
quantity           max 9,999        shape DECIMAL(4,0)
unit_price         max 999,999.99   shape DECIMAL(8,2)
discount_rate      max 1.0000       shape DECIMAL(5,4) plus a constraint limiting values to 0.0000 through 1.0000

Derived values:
gross_amount       9,999 * 999,999.99 = 9,998,999,900.01
                   integer digits 10, scale 2, shape DECIMAL(12,2)

line_discount      gross_amount * discount_rate
                   scale 2 + 4 = 6
                   max is gross_amount because rate <= 1.0000
                   integer digits 10, scale 6, shape DECIMAL(16,6)

line_net_exact     gross_amount - line_discount
                   bounded from 0 through gross_amount
                   integer digits 10, scale 6, shape DECIMAL(16,6)

Daily sum capacity:
max rows           2,000,000
extra digits       ceil(log10(2,000,000)) = 7
sum integer digits 10 + 7 = 17
sum scale          6
shape              DECIMAL(23,6)

sections.heading: Counterexamples that catch bad sizing
paragraphs: Counterexample one: using the row type for the aggregate. If gross_amount is DECIMAL(12, 2), a daily sum of gross_amount is not safely DECIMAL(12, 2). The row type can hold up to 9,998,999,900.01, but two million such rows can sum to 19,997,999,800,020,000.00. That requires 17 integer digits. A DECIMAL(12, 2) aggregate target has only ten integer digits and is off by seven digits.

Counterexample two: choosing DECIMAL(18, 2) because it looks large. DECIMAL(18, 2) has 16 integer digits. The hypothetical monthly gross maximum above has 18 integer digits. The declaration has many total digits, but not enough digits on the left side of the decimal point. This is why p alone is not meaningful; p minus s is the capacity that protects magnitude.

Counterexample three: multiplying by a rate and keeping only the money scale. Gross amount has scale 2 and discount_rate has scale 4, so the exact product has scale 6. If a pipeline casts the product directly into DECIMAL(12, 2), it may fit many ordinary rows but it has discarded four fractional digits from the calculation. Whether those digits should survive into a final reported amount is a separate rounding policy, but the intermediate shape should be chosen deliberately.

Counterexample four: trusting the declared rate type without enforcing the business domain. DECIMAL(5, 4) can describe a scale-4 value, but the type by itself does not express that a discount rate must be between zero and one. If the calculation relies on that bound to size discount_amount as DECIMAL(16, 6), then the bound belongs in validation, a check constraint, a data contract, or an upstream test. Otherwise the engineering assumption and the stored data can diverge.

sections.heading: A repeatable sizing procedure
paragraphs: The practical procedure is to size from the domain outward. Start with the smallest stored facts, then work through the expressions and aggregates they feed. Keep a short worksheet next to the model definition so a reviewer can see why each DECIMAL shape exists.

First, write the maximum magnitude and required fractional unit for every stored input. Avoid deriving this only from current data profiles. Observed maxima are useful diagnostics, but they are not capacity requirements unless the source system physically prevents larger values.

Second, write the expressions that create derived fields. For each expression, carry integer digits and scale through the operation. Multiplication is the expression most likely to surprise teams because the fractional scales add. Aggregation is the other common failure because row count becomes part of numeric capacity.

Third, separate storage shapes from calculation shapes. A source column, an intermediate expression, a fact-table field, and a dashboard output may all need different shapes. Narrowing a final output can be reasonable. Narrowing an intermediate value just because the final report shows fewer digits is a common source of reconciliation problems.

Fourth, document the operational cap used for aggregates. A daily table might be sized for the maximum order lines per day, while a customer lifetime table might be sized for the maximum retained history per customer. Duration and accumulating process facts have the same issue: a value that is safe per event may not be safe once accumulated across a long-running process.

Finally, add diagnostics that compare declared capacity to the model’s assumptions. The following SQL is illustrative, not execution evidence. It shows the kind of metadata query a PostgreSQL-oriented review might use to list decimal columns and their integer-digit capacity. PostgreSQL documentation for numeric types should be consulted for the exact behavior of the target version and for unconstrained numeric declarations.
bullets: For every decimal value, record maximum magnitude, scale, and the reason for both.
For every multiplication, add operand scales before choosing an intermediate type.
For every sum, include the maximum number of rows per group.
For every capacity assumption, decide whether it is enforced by a type, constraint, source contract, or validation test.
For every cast to a narrower decimal, name whether it is a storage limit, calculation limit, or presentation limit.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative PostgreSQL-oriented metadata diagnostic.
-- Purpose: list declared decimal shapes and integer digit capacity.
-- This does not prove the columns are correctly sized; it only exposes the declared capacity.

select
    table_schema,
    table_name,
    column_name,
    numeric_precision as precision_digits,
    numeric_scale as scale_digits,
    numeric_precision - numeric_scale as integer_digits
from information_schema.columns
where data_type = 'numeric'
  and numeric_precision is not null
  and numeric_scale is not null
order by table_schema, table_name, column_name;

sections.heading: Tradeoffs and review questions
paragraphs: Oversizing every decimal is not a free design principle. Wider numeric declarations can make schemas harder to reason about, can hide invalid upstream values, and may have storage or execution consequences depending on the database engine. Undersizing is worse when it causes overflow, silent narrowing, or inconsistent aggregate definitions. The goal is not maximum width; it is justified width.

The review question for a decimal column should not be only, will today’s data fit? Better questions are: what is the largest valid value, what intermediate expression can create a wider value, what is the largest group being summed, and what constraint enforces the bound? These questions turn precision and scale from guesswork into a small capacity model.

Measures of scale in statistics describe dispersion, but data modeling also needs a more mechanical sense of scale: the unit and magnitude a system can represent. Duration facts, lag facts, and other process measurements follow the same pattern as amounts. A per-event duration may fit comfortably in one type, while accumulated duration across a workflow or customer history may need a larger aggregate shape.

The safest habit is to keep capacity decisions close to the model. A comment, design note, or data contract entry that says daily_revenue_exact is DECIMAL(23, 6) because max line integer digits are 10, max rows are 2,000,000, and scale is 6 is much more useful than a bare DECIMAL(23, 6) with no rationale. Future maintainers can then update the type when the business maximum changes, instead of rediscovering the arithmetic during an incident.

takeaways: For DECIMAL(p, s), integer capacity is p minus s; always evaluate both sides of the decimal point.
Intermediate calculations can require wider shapes than stored source values, especially multiplication and aggregation.
For sums of positive values, include maximum group row count: integer digits need the row value’s integer digits plus ceil(log10(max rows)).
Business bounds such as discount_rate between 0 and 1 must be enforced somewhere if they are used to justify a smaller decimal type.
Document the arithmetic behind each important decimal declaration so capacity changes are intentional rather than accidental.

title: Integer overflow in aggregate calculations
description: A practical guide to estimating aggregate intermediate bounds so valid row-level values do not overflow sums, averages, rollups, and aggregate fact tables.
lead: Integer overflow in aggregate calculations is easy to miss because the individual rows can all be valid. The failure often appears one step later: a SUM accumulator, AVG numerator, rollup table, or derived expression exceeds the numeric type even though each input column is within its allowed range. The useful habit is to estimate bounds for intermediate values, not just source values.

sections.heading: Row ranges are not enough
paragraphs: A column-level range check answers a narrow question: can one value fit in this column? Aggregate correctness needs a different question: can the largest plausible intermediate value fit in the type used by the calculation? Those are not the same question.

Consider a hypothetical retail order-line table. Suppose quantity is allowed to range from 0 to 500 units, and unit_price_cents is allowed to range from 0 to 999,999 cents. Both numbers fit comfortably in a 32-bit signed integer. The row-level extended amount, quantity multiplied by unit_price_cents, has a maximum of 499,999,500 cents. That also fits inside a 32-bit signed integer whose maximum is 2,147,483,647.

Now aggregate those rows. Five maximum-sized lines sum to 2,499,997,500 cents, which exceeds the 32-bit signed integer maximum. Nothing illegal happened at the row level. The overflow risk appears only after the multiplication result is accumulated.

This is the counterexample that matters for data modeling: validating input domains does not validate aggregate domains. A model can be correct for storage and still be unsafe for analytics. Aggregate fact tables and cubes make this more important because they intentionally store precomputed summaries at coarser grains. Kimball’s guidance on aggregate fact tables emphasizes that aggregates are separate physical structures designed around a chosen grain; that grain change is also a numeric bound change.

The same issue appears in averages and ratios. An average order value may be small enough to fit in the final output type, but many systems compute it from a sum and a count. If the sum overflows before the division, the safe-looking final average is irrelevant. The design target is not only the displayed metric; it is every intermediate expression needed to compute that metric.

sections.heading: Rules for estimating intermediate bounds
paragraphs: The practical method is to write a bound for each operator in the calculation. Do this before choosing the storage type for a derived column, materialized aggregate, or semantic-layer metric.

For a nonnegative SUM, the upper bound is max_rows_per_group multiplied by max_value_per_row. If order_line_amount_cents is never negative, and the largest group can contain 80,000 lines, then the maximum group sum is 80,000 times the maximum line amount. If values can be negative, estimate both the most positive and most negative plausible sum. A signed type must hold both sides.

For a multiplication that feeds an aggregate, bound the product before bounding the sum. If both operands are nonnegative, multiply the maxima. If either operand can be negative, evaluate the endpoint combinations. For example, with a in [-10, 20] and b in [-3, 7], the product candidates are 30, -70, -60, and 140, so the product range is [-70, 140]. That product range, not either input range alone, becomes the input to the aggregate.

For AVG, do not stop at the final average range. Bound the numerator SUM and the denominator COUNT separately. Averages are particularly deceptive because the final value often remains in the same range as the input values, while the sum grows with row count.

For weighted averages, bound the weighted numerator and the weight denominator. If the metric is SUM(weight * value) / SUM(weight), the numerator can be much larger than either weight or value. If weights can be zero or negative, that is also a semantic issue, but the overflow calculation still starts with the product and the sums.

For rollups, repeat the calculation at every rollup grain. A daily store-sku aggregate may fit in a 64-bit integer, but a monthly category, annual region, or all-time company rollup multiplies the bound by more members. The maximum row count per group changes every time the grain changes.

For decimals, estimate required precision, not just scale. A decimal type with scale 2 preserves cents, but the precision must include the integer digits needed by the largest intermediate sum. If the largest possible dollar amount is 399,999,600,000.00, it needs 12 integer digits plus 2 fractional digits, so a precision of at least 14 with scale 2 is required for the value itself. Additional headroom may be appropriate if assumptions are uncertain.
bullets: Bound expressions before aggregates: product, discount, currency conversion, and allocation expressions can expand beyond their inputs.
Use maximum rows per calculation group, not average rows per group.
Compare against the accumulator type as well as the output column type.
Recompute bounds when the grain changes from line, to day, to month, to aggregate fact table.
Document whether the bound is contractual, operational, or merely historical.

sections.heading: Worked hypothetical retail example
paragraphs: Assume a hypothetical retail dataset called order_line_hypothetical. It is not based on a real customer or production system. The team wants to build a daily aggregate at the grain day, store_id, sku_id. The metric is gross_sales_cents = SUM(quantity * unit_price_cents).

The assumed constraints are: quantity is between 0 and 500; unit_price_cents is between 0 and 999,999; and a single day-store-sku group can contain at most 80,000 lines during a promotion or backfill-sized recomputation window. These are deliberately conservative assumptions for the example.

First calculate the row expression bound. The largest line amount is 500 multiplied by 999,999, which equals 499,999,500 cents. This fits in a 32-bit signed integer because 499,999,500 is less than 2,147,483,647.

Second calculate the aggregate bound. The largest daily group sum is 499,999,500 multiplied by 80,000, which equals 39,999,960,000,000 cents. This does not fit in a 32-bit signed integer. It does fit inside a 64-bit signed integer maximum of 9,223,372,036,854,775,807.

Third check the decimal representation if the model stores dollars instead of cents. The aggregate cents amount is 399,999,600,000.00 dollars. That requires 12 integer digits and 2 fractional digits. A decimal type that allows only 10 integer digits with 2 decimal places is not enough, even though it may have looked reasonable for normal daily reporting.

This small example shows the failure mode clearly: the input columns and row expression pass a 32-bit check, but the aggregate does not. The safe design is based on the group-level bound, not the source column range.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative SQL for documenting an aggregate bound.
-- Adapt numeric type names and casting rules to your warehouse or database.
WITH assumptions AS (
  SELECT
    500 AS max_quantity,
    999999 AS max_unit_price_cents,
    80000 AS max_lines_per_day_store_sku,
    2147483647 AS int32_max,
    9223372036854775807 AS int64_max
), bounds AS (
  SELECT
    max_quantity * max_unit_price_cents AS max_line_amount_cents,
    max_quantity * max_unit_price_cents * max_lines_per_day_store_sku AS max_group_amount_cents,
    int32_max,
    int64_max
  FROM assumptions
)
SELECT
  max_line_amount_cents,
  max_group_amount_cents,
  CASE
    WHEN max_group_amount_cents > int32_max THEN 'int32 unsafe for aggregate'
    ELSE 'int32 sufficient for aggregate'
  END AS int32_assessment,
  CASE
    WHEN max_group_amount_cents > int64_max THEN 'int64 unsafe for aggregate'
    ELSE 'int64 sufficient for aggregate'
  END AS int64_assessment
FROM bounds;

sections.heading: A diagnostic for real models
paragraphs: A useful diagnostic is to create a numeric bound sheet for each important aggregate. It can live as a design note, a data contract appendix, or a small table used by tests. The point is not to predict the exact future; it is to expose hidden multipliers before they become overflow bugs.

Start with the business grain. For example: one row per order line, one aggregate per day-store-sku, one rollup per fiscal month-category, or one customer lifetime metric. Then list the expression being aggregated. Avoid vague metric names such as revenue; write quantity * unit_price_cents, SUM(line_amount_cents), or SUM(weight * score).

Next, assign a bound source to each assumption. A contractual bound is strongest: for example, an application validation rule that rejects quantity above 500. An operational bound is weaker but still useful: for example, a capacity limit that makes more than 80,000 lines per day-store-sku implausible. A historical maximum is the weakest because tomorrow can exceed yesterday. Historical profiling is useful for finding surprises, but it should not be the only bound for a durable data model.

Then compare the bound to the actual type used by the calculation. This requires reading your engine’s documentation because aggregate return types and decimal behavior vary. PostgreSQL’s documentation, for example, separates numeric type definitions from aggregate function behavior; practitioners should check both the numeric type page and the aggregate function page for the exact version they run. The broader lesson is durable across systems: the input column type, accumulator type, and output type may not be identical.

Finally, include a counterexample row set in validation. The fixture does not need to be large. If five maximum-sized rows overflow a 32-bit sum, a unit-style test can demonstrate the risk without generating 80,000 rows. If the intended safety claim is about 64-bit or decimal precision, use the calculated bound value directly and assert that the model can represent it.
bullets: Name the grain being bounded.
Name the exact expression being accumulated.
Record max rows per group and where that assumption comes from.
Check expression type, aggregate accumulator type, and stored output type.
Keep at least one adversarial fixture that reaches the calculated edge case.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative adversarial fixture using the hypothetical retail assumptions.
-- The expected total is 2,499,997,500 cents for five rows.
-- That value is greater than a signed 32-bit integer maximum.
WITH order_line_hypothetical(quantity, unit_price_cents) AS (
  SELECT 500, 999999 UNION ALL
  SELECT 500, 999999 UNION ALL
  SELECT 500, 999999 UNION ALL
  SELECT 500, 999999 UNION ALL
  SELECT 500, 999999
)
SELECT
  SUM(quantity * unit_price_cents) AS gross_sales_cents
FROM order_line_hypothetical;

sections.heading: Design tradeoffs and countermeasures
paragraphs: The simplest countermeasure is to use a wider exact numeric type for aggregate inputs and outputs. Integer cents stored in 64-bit signed integers are often easier to reason about than binary floating point for exact counted units, but the 64-bit range is still finite. Decimal types can be clearer when fractional units are part of the domain, but precision must be sized for the largest intermediate result, not just the prettiest display format.

Casting only at the end is often too late. If quantity * unit_price_cents is evaluated in a narrow type before SUM sees it, the product can overflow before the aggregate receives the value. Cast or model the expression so the widening happens before the risky operation. The same principle applies to SUM before AVG, multiplication before weighted averages, and daily aggregates before monthly rollups.

Another countermeasure is to reduce the maximum group size by changing the grain of materialization, but that is a modeling decision, not just a numeric trick. Storing daily store-sku aggregates may keep one calculation within range, while a later annual rollup still needs its own bound. Aggregate fact tables improve performance and usability when designed well, but they do not remove the need to size numeric fields for the aggregate grain.

Do not use floating point merely to avoid integer overflow in exact financial or unit-count metrics. Floating point has its own representation behavior and is a separate correctness topic. When the requirement is exact cents, counts, or units, solve the aggregate bound explicitly with an exact type that has enough range.

The practical rule is conservative: if the metric is important enough to persist or publish, write down the maximum intermediate value that could occur. A one-line formula such as max_rows_per_group times max_line_amount catches many bugs that ordinary schema checks miss.

takeaways: Check aggregate intermediate bounds, not just source column ranges. Valid rows can still produce an overflowing SUM, AVG numerator, weighted numerator, or rollup.
For each metric, bound the expression first, then multiply by the maximum rows per group at the relevant grain.
Accumulator type matters. Verify the expression type, aggregate return type, and stored output type for the database or warehouse you use.
Decimal scale is not enough; precision must include the integer digits required by the largest intermediate value.
Use small adversarial fixtures to make overflow risk visible before it reaches production data volumes.

title: Unit conversions in analytical models
description: A practical guide to preserving original units and conversion provenance beside normalized values in analytical models, with counterexamples and calculation rules for data engineers.
lead: Unit conversions in analytical models are not just formatting choices. If a fact arrives as 3 pounds, 48 ounces, 1 case, or 750 milliliters, the model needs a normalized value for comparison and aggregation, but it also needs the original value, original unit, and conversion rule that produced the normalized value. Without that provenance, teams cannot explain small numeric differences, repair a bad conversion rule, or distinguish a true business change from a unit-handling bug.

sections.heading: Why normalized-only is not enough
paragraphs: A common modeling shortcut is to convert every incoming measurement to a preferred reporting unit and keep only the converted number. For example, a pipeline may turn pounds and ounces into grams, liters and milliliters into liters, or cases and packs into eaches. That makes downstream queries simpler, but it also destroys evidence needed to answer a basic audit question: what did the source system actually send, and which rule changed it?

The safer pattern is to store both sides of the conversion: the source-side measurement and the analytic-side measurement. The source-side fields are treated as immutable facts. The normalized fields are derived facts. The conversion rule is not hidden in application code; it is represented in data, with an identifier that can be joined, inspected, and versioned.

Kimball’s dimensional modeling guidance on multiple units of measure supports the idea that warehouses often need to represent compatible facts in more than one unit. Kimball’s Type 0 “retain original” technique is also a useful mental model here: some attributes should preserve their original captured value rather than being overwritten when downstream interpretation changes. Applied to unit conversion, the original quantity and unit should not be replaced by the normalized quantity and unit.

This article is limited to physical or operational measurements such as weight, volume, length, duration, and product-specific package quantities. It does not cover tax, accounting treatment, or currency conversion-date policy. It also assumes the reader already understands why exact numeric representation matters and why binary floating point can create avoidable surprises in analytical arithmetic.

sections.heading: A hypothetical counterexample: rounding hides the conversion error
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail fulfillment dataset where small spice refill picks are captured by a warehouse device in pounds. The analytics model reports mass in grams. The correct conversion factor is 453.59237 grams per pound.

Suppose 10,000 pick events are each recorded as 0.005 pounds. If the model first aggregates the original pounds and then converts, the calculation is 10,000 × 0.005 = 50 pounds. Converted to grams, 50 × 453.59237 = 22,679.6185 grams.

Now compare that with a pipeline that converts each row to grams, rounds the normalized value to two decimal places, stores only that rounded value, and discards the original fields. Each event becomes 0.005 × 453.59237 = 2.26796185 grams, rounded to 2.27 grams. Summed across 10,000 events, the reported value is 22,700.00 grams.

The difference is 22,700.00 − 22,679.6185 = 20.3815 grams. That may or may not matter for a specific business decision, but the modeling problem is clear: if only 2.27 grams is stored, the model cannot explain whether the difference came from source precision, a conversion factor, per-row rounding, or a later aggregation. The normalized number is useful, but it is not sufficient evidence.

The rule is simple: preserve the original measurement at source precision, preserve the conversion rule, compute normalized values with adequate decimal precision, and round only at the presentation boundary unless a metric definition explicitly requires earlier rounding.
bullets: Original input: 10,000 events × 0.005 pounds = 50 pounds.
Conversion factor: 453.59237 grams per pound.
Aggregate-then-convert result: 22,679.6185 grams.
Convert-then-round-per-row result: 22,700.00 grams.
Rounding difference: 20.3815 grams.

sections.heading: Model the measurement and the rule
paragraphs: A unit-aware fact table should carry enough information to answer four questions: what value arrived, what unit arrived, what value was used for analysis, and what rule produced it. This can be done without making every query complicated. Analysts usually query the normalized value. Data engineers and metric owners can inspect the provenance fields when results look wrong.

A practical grain for the conversion rule is the smallest level at which the rule is valid. For universal multiplicative conversions, such as pounds to grams, the rule may depend only on the source unit and target unit. For product packaging, such as cases to eaches, the rule often depends on the product. One product’s case may contain 12 units; another product’s case may contain 24. Treating “case” as a universal unit is a common source of quiet overcounting or undercounting.

The model below is illustrative SQL, not a claim about a specific database engine. The important part is not the exact syntax. The important part is that original values, normalized values, and conversion-rule identity are all first-class data.
bullets: Store original_quantity as received, using a decimal type appropriate for the source precision.
Store original_unit_code or original_unit_key, not just a label in a report.
Store normalized_quantity and normalized_unit_code for common aggregation.
Store conversion_rule_key so the normalized value can be traced back to a rule version.
For multiplicative conversions, store the multiplier as exact decimal components where practical, such as numerator and denominator or a sufficiently precise DECIMAL value.
For package conversions, include the product or package context in the rule key; do not assume the unit name alone is enough.
For affine or non-linear conversions, such as units with offsets or formulas, store the expression type and parameters, not only a multiplier.

codeExamples.code:
-- Illustrative schema for a unit-aware analytical model.
-- Syntax may need adjustment for a specific warehouse.

CREATE TABLE dim_unit (
  unit_key            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  unit_code           VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL,
  measurement_family  VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL,
  unit_name           VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE dim_unit_conversion_rule (
  conversion_rule_key INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  from_unit_key       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  to_unit_key         INTEGER NOT NULL,
  conversion_type     VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL, -- multiplicative, package, affine
  product_key         INTEGER NULL,
  multiplier_decimal  DECIMAL(38, 18) NULL,
  offset_decimal      DECIMAL(38, 18) NULL,
  valid_from_date     DATE NOT NULL,
  valid_to_date       DATE NULL,
  rule_source         VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
  rule_version        VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE fact_fulfillment_measurement (
  event_key             BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  event_timestamp       TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  product_key           INTEGER NOT NULL,
  original_quantity     DECIMAL(38, 12) NOT NULL,
  original_unit_key     INTEGER NOT NULL,
  normalized_quantity   DECIMAL(38, 12) NOT NULL,
  normalized_unit_key   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  conversion_rule_key   INTEGER NOT NULL
);

sections.heading: Calculation rules that prevent ambiguous aggregates
paragraphs: The model should be accompanied by explicit calculation rules. Otherwise, two teams can use the same tables and still produce different totals. The rules below are intentionally mechanical so they can be implemented in transformation code, reviewed in pull requests, and tested with small fixtures.

First, aggregate compatible normalized values, not raw original quantities, unless all rows have the same unit and the metric definition says the original unit is the reporting unit. Summing 3 pounds and 16 ounces as if both numbers were just “quantity” produces 19, which is neither pounds nor ounces. The normalized field exists to prevent that mistake.

Second, do not aggregate across measurement families. A mass, a volume, a duration, and a count are not interchangeable because they share a numeric type. A query that sums normalized_weight_grams and normalized_volume_milliliters is syntactically possible in many warehouses, but analytically meaningless. Unit metadata gives you a way to reject or diagnose this.

Third, distinguish universal unit conversions from product-specific packaging conversions. In a hypothetical customer-order model, Product A may define 1 case = 12 eaches, while Product B defines 1 case = 24 eaches. If a transformation applies a global rule that 1 case = 12 eaches, then an order for 1 case of Product B is understated by 12 eaches. The source row might look harmless because the original quantity is just 1 and the unit is just “case”; the missing detail is that the conversion rule must include product context.

Fourth, do not let display rounding become storage rounding. If the dashboard needs kilograms with one decimal place, round in the semantic layer or final select. The fact table should keep enough precision to support different future aggregations, diagnostics, and reconciliations.

Fifth, make recalculation possible. A reviewer should be able to join the fact row to the rule row and recompute the normalized value within a defined tolerance. If a rule later changes, do not silently overwrite historical original values. Either keep the historical rule for reproducibility or create a new derived version with a new rule key.
bullets: Rule 1: Convert to a declared normalized unit before cross-unit aggregation.
Rule 2: Reject aggregations that mix measurement families.
Rule 3: Treat packaging conversions as product-specific unless proven otherwise.
Rule 4: Store precise normalized values; round for presentation.
Rule 5: Keep conversion rules versioned and joinable from facts.
Rule 6: Recalculate from provenance during data quality checks.

sections.heading: Diagnostics for existing models
paragraphs: If a model already contains measurements, the fastest diagnostic is to look for places where a quantity column is aggregated without a unit column nearby. Another warning sign is a normalized value with no original value. That design may be acceptable for a source that natively reports only one unit, but it is risky when the ingestion layer performs conversions before loading the warehouse.

The following SQL examples are illustrative. They show the type of checks a data engineer can adapt to a specific schema. The first query finds reporting groups where raw original quantities would be unsafe to sum because multiple original units appear in the same group. The second query checks whether stored normalized values still match the recorded conversion rule for multiplicative conversions.
These diagnostics are not substitutes for metric definitions. They are guardrails that reveal whether the model has enough information for a metric definition to be executed consistently.

codeExamples.code:
-- Diagnostic 1: groups where raw original quantities mix units.
-- If this returns rows, use normalized quantities for aggregation.

SELECT
  product_key,
  CAST(event_timestamp AS DATE) AS event_date,
  COUNT(DISTINCT original_unit_key) AS original_unit_count,
  SUM(original_quantity) AS unsafe_sum_of_original_quantity,
  SUM(normalized_quantity) AS safe_sum_of_normalized_quantity
FROM fact_fulfillment_measurement
GROUP BY product_key, CAST(event_timestamp AS DATE)
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT original_unit_key) > 1;

-- Diagnostic 2: verify multiplicative conversions against the stored rule.
-- The tolerance should be chosen by the metric owner based on stored precision.

SELECT
  f.event_key,
  f.original_quantity,
  f.normalized_quantity,
  r.multiplier_decimal,
  (f.original_quantity * r.multiplier_decimal) AS recalculated_normalized_quantity,
  ABS(f.normalized_quantity - (f.original_quantity * r.multiplier_decimal)) AS absolute_difference
FROM fact_fulfillment_measurement f
JOIN dim_unit_conversion_rule r
  ON f.conversion_rule_key = r.conversion_rule_key
WHERE r.conversion_type = 'multiplicative'
  AND ABS(f.normalized_quantity - (f.original_quantity * r.multiplier_decimal)) > 0.000001;

sections.heading: When to store more than one normalized value
paragraphs: A single normalized unit is usually enough within one measurement family: grams for mass, milliliters for volume, seconds for duration, or eaches for item counts. However, some analytical models benefit from storing more than one derived representation. For example, a logistics model may store weight in grams for exact aggregation and kilograms for common operational reporting. If both are stored, both should point to the same conversion provenance or to separately identified derivation rules.

Do not create multiple normalized columns just because different dashboards prefer different labels. A dashboard can divide grams by 1,000 to display kilograms. Store another normalized value only when it has a distinct grain, rule, precision requirement, or audit purpose.

The key design test is whether a future maintainer can explain a number from the table alone. If normalized_weight_kg is present, the table should reveal whether it was computed from pounds, ounces, grams, or a package rule; which factor was used; and whether it was rounded before storage. If that explanation requires reading old transformation code or asking the original developer, the model is missing provenance.

sections.heading: Implementation checklist
paragraphs: A robust unit-conversion design is not complicated, but it must be deliberate. The mistake is to treat unit conversion as a one-time cleanup step instead of an analytical contract. The contract says that normalized values are available for consistent reporting, while original values and conversion rules remain available for explanation and correction.
Use the following checklist when adding a measurement to a model or reviewing an existing one.
bullets: Declare the measurement family: mass, volume, length, duration, count, package, or another explicit family.
Choose the canonical analytical unit for that family and document why it is the aggregation unit.
Preserve original_quantity and original_unit as immutable source-side facts.
Compute normalized_quantity using DECIMAL arithmetic with sufficient precision for the metric.
Store normalized_unit, even if there is only one expected normalized unit today.
Join every derived normalized value to a conversion_rule_key.
Version conversion rules instead of overwriting them in place.
Include product, package, location, or supplier context when the conversion depends on that context.
Define where rounding is allowed and where it is forbidden.
Add diagnostics that recalculate normalized values from original values and conversion rules.

takeaways: A normalized measurement is useful for analytics, but it should not replace the original quantity and unit captured from the source.
Conversion provenance should be modeled as data: rule key, source unit, target unit, conversion type, parameters, context, and version.
Small rounding choices can become visible at scale, so store sufficient precision and round only where the metric definition requires it.
Package units such as cases and packs are often product-specific; treating them as universal units creates silent aggregate errors.
A good unit-conversion model lets engineers recalculate normalized values from original values and explain differences without reading old pipeline code.
